questions.question: Which sequence correctly describes the major overlapping phases of wound healing?
questions.explanation: Wound healing is commonly described as overlapping phases of hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and remodeling.

questions.question: Which cell is especially important in the transition from inflammatory cleanup to coordinated repair?
questions.explanation: Macrophages clear debris and coordinate cytokine/growth-factor signaling that supports repair, angiogenesis, and fibroblast activity.

questions.question: Which process is most characteristic of the proliferative phase?
choices: Angiogenesis, fibroblast matrix production, granulation tissue, and re-epithelialization
Complete return to normal tissue architecture
questions.explanation: The proliferative phase features new-vessel formation, fibroblast activity, extracellular-matrix deposition, granulation tissue, and epithelial coverage.

questions.question: Why does poor arterial perfusion impair wound healing?
choices: It increases oxygen delivery to the wound
It reduces oxygen delivery required for cellular function, collagen synthesis, and host defense
It eliminates the need for angiogenesis
questions.explanation: Adequate perfusion supports oxygen-dependent cellular repair, collagen synthesis, immune defense, and angiogenesis. Ischemia delays healing and raises tissue-loss risk.

questions.question: A clean surgical incision with closely approximated edges heals with less granulation tissue and scarring. This is:
questions.explanation: Primary-intention healing occurs when clean wound edges are closely approximated. Secondary intention requires more tissue filling, contraction, and scar.

questions.question: A patient with diabetes has a plantar ulcer beneath a pressure point and reduced protective sensation. What mechanism is most central?
questions.explanation: Neuropathy can eliminate protective sensation, allowing repeated pressure and trauma. Diabetes may also add perfusion and infection-risk contributors.

questions.question: Which is the safest approach to a chronic wound in a patient with diabetes?
choices: Call every lesion a diabetic ulcer and treat the surface only
Assess wound characteristics plus pulses/perfusion, sensation, pressure, edema, infection signs, glycemic context, and systemic risk
Use the same dressing and antibiotics for every wound
Avoid neurovascular assessment if the wound is painless
questions.explanation: Chronic wounds are often multifactorial. A complete wound and neurovascular assessment is needed to identify arterial, venous, neuropathic, pressure, infectious, and systemic contributors.

questions.question: A patient with a chronic foot wound now has fever, rapidly expanding erythema, severe pain, and dusky skin. What is the key FNP decision?
choices: Recognize possible deep/necrotizing infection and arrange emergency evaluation
Assume the pain excludes neuropathy and no further workup is needed
questions.explanation: Systemic symptoms, rapid progression, severe pain, and skin discoloration are red flags for a potentially limb- or life-threatening infection and require emergency escalation.

questions.question: Which statement best describes fibrosis?
choices: Replacement with normal tissue architecture in every organ
Persistent repair signaling with excess extracellular-matrix/collagen deposition that can impair function
A process limited to skin wounds
A condition caused only by acute infection
questions.explanation: Fibrosis is excess matrix/collagen deposition during persistent injury and repair. It can distort architecture and reduce function in skin, liver, kidney, lung, heart, and other tissues.

questions.question: Why should a chronic lower-extremity wound not automatically be treated with one generic intervention?
choices: All chronic wounds have identical mechanisms
Etiology may include arterial insufficiency, venous hypertension/edema, neuropathy, pressure, infection, and systemic contributors; management must target the cause
Perfusion has no relation to healing
Wound depth and systemic symptoms are not clinically important
questions.explanation: Chronic wounds are commonly multifactorial. Determining etiology and neurovascular status is necessary before cause-directed management and appropriate referral.
